pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Recording data of increasing complexity (graphs & keys)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires "recording data and results of increasing complexity using scientific diagrams and labels, classification keys, tables, scatter graphs, bar and line graphs" (verbatim). The step-up from lower KS2 is LINE and SCATTER graphs and choosing the appropriate type.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 4 Analyzing & Interpreting Data, grades 3–5 into 6–8):** the 3–5 progression covers representing data graphically to reveal patterns; the 6–8 progression adds constructing and interpreting graphical displays (including line graphs) to identify linear and nonlinear relationships. Selecting and accurately plotting the right graph type sits on this boundary.

- **Operational details:** Builds on basic tables/bar charts/keys (prerequisite mt_7IFpDVNsmt) and maths discrete/continuous graphing (mt_ChjMU2GDJa). Three moves: (1) CHOOSE the appropriate graph — bar chart for categories, LINE graph for continuous change (e.g. over time), scatter graph for relationship between two continuous variables; (2) draw it with correctly LABELLED AXES, sensible SCALES, and accurate plotting; and (3) use classification keys and scientific diagrams for complex findings. The pivotal new idea is that continuous data (a variable that changes smoothly) wants a line graph, whereas categories want bars. Feeds forward to KS3 best-fit lines/gradients and causal reporting (dependents mt_YHsUhi4Prc, mt_nyPMkeHlVJ).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). A learner who can select the correct graph type for a dataset, plot it accurately with labelled axes and an appropriate scale, and use keys/diagrams for complex findings has met the bar. Lines of best fit and gradients are the KS3 tier (mt_YHsUhi4Prc).
bestPractices: Teach graph-type SELECTION on the nature of the data: categories → bar chart; one continuous variable changing (often over time) → line graph; relationship between two continuous variables → scatter — give datasets that force the choice rather than pre-deciding.

Make axis choice a taught decision: which variable goes on x (the one you changed / independent) and y (the one you measured / dependent), plus choosing a scale that uses the grid well — a common failure point.
Confront the continuous-vs-discrete distinction directly, since drawing a line through category (discrete) data or a bar chart of continuous data is the signature upper-KS2 error.
Have pupils plot from their OWN fair-test data so the graph answers a real question and links back to the experimental-design spine.
Use accurate plotting as a habit (read the value, find the coordinate, mark precisely) and check by reading a point back off the graph.
keyRepresentations: A graph-type chooser keyed to data type (categorical / continuous-over-time / two-variable relationship)
A line graph with independent variable on x, dependent on y, labelled axes and units
A scatter graph showing a relationship between two continuous variables
A scale-choosing exercise (spread the data across the grid)
A branching classification key for complex specimens
commonMisconceptions: Drawing a line graph through discrete/categorical data (joining bars that shouldn't be joined), or a bar chart for continuous data.
Putting the wrong variable on each axis, or not distinguishing the changed (independent) from the measured (dependent) variable.
Choosing a scale that squashes the data into a corner or that isn't linear/even, distorting the pattern.
Omitting axis labels or units so the graph can't be interpreted.
Plotting inaccurately or reading points off carelessly, then trusting the resulting shape.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, learners record data of increasing complexity by choosing the right graph for the nature of the data, plotting it with labelled axes, units and an even scale on each numerical axis, and building classification keys. The pivotal idea: categorical data suits bar charts; a continuous variable tracked as another continuous variable changes (most often time) suits a line graph; and two measured continuous variables checked for a relationship suit a scatter graph. The wrong choice can bury or misrepresent the pattern; the right choice makes it easier to read. Plotting one's own fair-test data is encouraged so the graph answers a real question.

activities.title: Plot your own data: choosing type, axes and scale
feedback: If a line is drawn through categorical data (joining bars that shouldn't be joined), point out that these points aren't connected — sort the data as categories versus continuous first, then re-choose the graph type before drawing.
If the scale is spaced by the order the numbers were collected rather than by value, note that equal gaps must mean equal amounts; mark the whole axis before plotting any point.

If the scale squashes the data into a corner, suggest using fewer units per square so the data fills the grid and any pattern is easier to see; on a bar chart, keep the count axis starting at zero so the bar heights can still be compared fairly.
If axes carry numbers but no quantity name or unit, require each axis to name what was measured and its unit before the graph is 'finished'; check against the data-table headings.
Ask: why did you pick this graph type rather than a bar chart / line graph for this data? If someone else read it, would they know what each axis measures and in what units — show me where.
activities.rationale: Graph-type selection and accurate construction are the step-up skills at upper KS2 and on the NGSS 3–5 into 6–8 boundary. Forcing the choice on datasets of different natures, and making the axis and scale decisions explicit, is intended to target the signature errors (lines through discrete data, uneven scales, missing labels). Plotting one's own fair-test data ties the graph back to a real question. The cited standards establish that these graph and key skills are required at this stage; they do not by themselves establish the efficacy of this proposed design.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires recording data and results of increasing complexity using scientific diagrams and labels, classification keys, tables, scatter graphs, bar and line graphs.
NGSS SEP 4 progresses from representing data graphically to reveal patterns (3-5) to constructing and interpreting graphical displays to identify linear and nonlinear relationships (6-8).
learnerActions: Take a real dataset — ideally from your own fair test (e.g. a plant's height measured each week) — plus a categorical set (e.g. favourite-fruit counts) and a two-variable set.

Decide for each dataset whether the data is categorical, a continuous variable tracked as it changes over time (or as another continuous variable changes), or two measured continuous variables checked for a relationship.

Choose the graph type: bar chart for categories, line graph for a continuous variable tracked as it changes over time (or as another continuous variable changes), scatter graph for two measured continuous variables where you are looking for a relationship.

Put the changed/independent variable (or the categories, for a bar chart) on the x-axis and the measured/dependent variable on the y-axis; if a scatter graph compares two measured variables and neither was changed, choose one for each axis and say which. Label each axis with the quantity AND its unit where it has one.

Mark the scale on each numerical axis FIRST — equal squares for equal amounts — choosing a scale that spreads the data across the grid rather than squashing it into a corner; on a bar chart, space the categories evenly and start the count axis at zero.
Plot each point accurately (read the value, find the coordinate, mark precisely), then check by reading one point back off the graph against the data table.

Deliberately try plotting the categorical data as a line graph and notice that the joining lines suggest in-between values that don't exist, and that the line's shape changes if you reorder the categories; compare with the correct bar chart.
activities.intendedInsight: A graph isn't a decoration added at the end — the right choice of type, axes and scale is what lets the data tell its story, while the wrong one can hide the pattern or imply connections that don't exist.

activities.title: Build and test a classification key
feedback: If questions are vague or non-binary, or two organisms end at the same point, rework them: every question must be an observable yes/no that divides the remaining set.
Prompt: run this organism through your key — does every question have a clear yes or no answer? What happens if two look the same?
activities.rationale: Using classification keys and scientific diagrams for complex findings is part of the recording-complex-data standard. Testing the key against each specimen exposes non-distinguishing questions, which is where keys commonly fail.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires recording data and results of increasing complexity using scientific diagrams and labels, classification keys, tables, scatter graphs, bar and line graphs.
learnerActions: Take a small set of organisms (or specimens) to sort by observable features.
Write a sequence of yes/no questions, each about an observable feature, that splits the remaining set at every step.
Draw the key as a branching structure so each organism reaches its own endpoint.
Test the key by running every organism through it, checking that each question has a clear yes or no answer and that no two organisms end at the same point.
If two specimens look the same at a step, add a finer observable question that separates them.
activities.intendedInsight: A working key is built from clear, binary, observable distinctions that divide a set until every specimen is uniquely identified.

activities.title: Read, judge and correct graphs (checks and references)
feedback: For a value-reading task, check the answer against the plotted coordinate; if wrong, retrace reading the axis then finding the point.
For error-spotting, confirm the identified fault (missing unit, uneven interval, wrong type) and the proposed fix.
Remember: recognising the right graph or spotting an error checks understanding but does not by itself show you can construct and choose a graph independently — pair it with the plotting activity.
activities.rationale: Recognition, value-reading and error-spotting are efficient checks and make useful references, but they assess or support rather than require independent construction, so they complement the hands-on plotting task rather than replace it.
learnerActions: Given a line graph, read a specified value off the axes accurately.
Given graphs with mislabelled or unevenly-scaled axes, spot and describe the error and say how to fix it.
Decide which graph type suits a described dataset and justify the choice.
Use a tap-to-reveal reference showing when to use a bar chart vs line graph vs scatter as a support while deciding — not as a substitute for constructing your own.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to read values and diagnose scale/label errors in others' graphs reinforces what makes your own graph interpretable.

constraints: Lines of best fit and gradients belong to the later (KS3) tier and are beyond this bar; the target here is selecting the correct graph, plotting accurately with labelled axes and an even scale, and building a working key.

Builds on prior work with basic tables, bar charts and keys, and on maths discrete/continuous graphing; learners who sort data by type incorrectly may need to revisit the discrete-vs-continuous distinction first.

A static annotated exemplar or tap-to-reveal reference supports recall of when to use each graph type but does not itself require the learner to make the choice, assign axes, set a scale and plot — treat it as a scaffold alongside construction.
Recognition and error-spotting tasks check or diagnose understanding but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a graph or key.

Interactive examples (e.g. a live plotter that draws a flagged zig-zag when a line is chosen for categories, or lets a cramped scale be stretched to reveal a hidden trend) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete and add immediate feedback; squared paper, a dataset and the learner's own plotting are an equally valid route to the same independent-construction goal.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One cited source (NGSS Appendix F progression) is marked verified:false in the original row; treat the 3–5 into 6–8 boundary claim with that caveat. The DfE and NGSS claims support the standards-placement framing only, not the efficacy of any proposed activity.

The original framed a live graphing studio as teaching selection 'viscerally' with wrong-choice flagging as the core mechanism; this has been retained as an optional interaction example rather than a necessary or superior medium, since comparative efficacy is not established by the source claims.

probeDeeper: Why did you pick this graph type rather than a bar chart / line graph for this data?
If someone read your graph, would they know what each axis measures and in what units? Show me where.
Run this organism through your key — does every question have a clear yes or no answer? What happens if two look the same?
assess.correctAnswer: The child selects a graph type suited to the data (line graph for the continuous week-by-week height; bar chart for categorical counts; scatter for two continuous variables), draws axes labelled with quantities and units, uses an even, linear scale, plots accurately, and constructs a key from a sequence of yes/no questions on observable features that separates every organism.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong graph type for the data — e.g. a bar chart for continuous time data, or joins categorical bars into a line.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort data as categories versus continuous first, then map each to its graph type; re-choose before drawing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Graph form doesn't match the data type (line for categories, or bars for a continuous trend).

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses an uneven scale — spaces the axis by the order the numbers were collected rather than by value, so equal gaps mean unequal amounts.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the scale before plotting any point: equal squares equal equal amounts; mark the axis first, then plot.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Axis intervals are irregular; data points are evenly spaced regardless of their values.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits axis labels or units, so the graph doesn't say what was measured.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Require each axis to name the quantity and its unit before the graph is 'finished'; check against the data table headings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Axes carry numbers but no quantity name or unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a key from non-distinguishing or overlapping questions (vague or non-binary), so it fails to separate the organisms.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test the key by running each organism through it; every question must be an observable yes/no that divides the remaining set.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Key questions aren't clear yes/no splits on observable features, or two organisms end at the same point.

responseLevels.gap: Wrong graph type, uneven or missing scale, unlabelled axes; key questions don't reliably separate the organisms.
responseLevels.full: Chooses the appropriate graph, labels axes with units on an even scale and plots accurately, and constructs a working key of clear yes/no observable questions that identifies every organism.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the graph type right and plots reasonably but slips on scale, labels, or units; or builds a key that works for most but has a vague or overlapping question.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a set of results from an investigation [provide a dataset — e.g. a plant's height measured each week, plus a mix of organisms to sort]. Present these properly: choose the right kind of graph and draw it with labelled axes, sensible scales, and accurate points, and build a classification key that would let someone else identify each organism. (Provide squared paper and the data; watch the choices the child makes.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the construction reveals judgements a finished-graph glance would hide: whether the child CHOSE the right graph for the data type, whether the scale is even or spaced by data order, and whether the key's questions actually split the set. These process choices are exactly where increasing-complexity data recording succeeds or fails.
